content: Drooling is a frequent issue among children with cerebral palsy (CP), and it can cause significant distress not only for the affected children but also for their parents and caregivers. The consequences of drooling are multifaceted and include the risk of social rejection, persistent dampness and soiling of clothing, unpleasant odors, irritation and chapping of the skin, oral infections, dehydration, interference with speech, and damage to personal items such as books, communication aids, and computers. Additionally, drooling can contribute to social isolation. Various interventions have been developed to address drooling, aiming to reduce or eliminate it. However, there is no consensus on which interventions are the most effective for children with CP. The objectives of this review were threefold: to assess the effectiveness and safety of interventions for drooling in children with CP, to provide the best available evidence to guide clinical practice, and to assist in planning future research. To achieve these objectives, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, covering the period from their inception to December 2010. The databases included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Medline via Ovid, EMBASE, CINAHL, ERIC, PsychINFO, Web of Science, Web of Knowledge, AMED, SCOPUS, and Dissertation Abstracts. Ongoing clinical trials were also identified through ClinicalTrials.gov and the Current Controlled Trials website. Additionally, relevant journals and conference proceedings were manually searched. The review included only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials (CCTs). Data extraction was performed independently by three reviewers, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Six studies met the inclusion criteria for the review. Four of these studies investigated the use of botulinum toxin-A (BoNT-A), while the remaining two focused on pharmacological interventions using benztropine and glycopyrrolate. No RCTs or CCTs were identified for other interventions such as surgery, physical therapies, oro-motor and oro-sensory therapies, behavioral interventions, intra-oral appliances, or acupuncture. The included studies exhibited significant heterogeneity both within and across the interventions, which precluded the possibility of conducting a meta-analysis. Instead, a descriptive summary of each study was provided. All six studies demonstrated some statistically significant improvements in the treatment groups, but these effects were observed only up to one month after the intervention. Importantly, all six studies had methodological limitations. The authors concluded that it was not possible to determine the effectiveness and safety of either BoNT-A or the pharmaceutical interventions (benztropine and glycopyrrolate) based on the available evidence. Consequently, there is insufficient evidence to guide clinical practice regarding interventions for drooling in children with CP. The review also highlighted the need for further research in this area and provided recommendations for future studies.
